title: Joiner edits relationship details and gets an unexplained failure
preconditions: A created the space; B joined as the partner.
B opens Account and chooses Edit relationship.
B changes the anniversary date and saves.

actions.note: B opens Edit relationship and saves a new date.

expected_behavior: A non-creator is either not offered the edit action or told plainly that only the creator can change space details.
A failed save explains the rule and preserves the current values.
The UI never implies that the partner's change was saved.
candidate_failure_modes: The partner taps a working-looking Edit relationship row, fills the form, and receives only "Unable to save. Please try again."
The partner retries because the message implies a transient network problem.
The partner believes the anniversary date changed when the server rejected it.

observed_code_behavior: Spaces enforce one active membership per user and one active partner per space at the storage layer.
Joining redeems an invite once; an expired or already-redeemed code is rejected, and a historical partner slot is permanently bound.
Leaving flips the caller's membership to left and keeps shared history for the remaining member.
Space hydration, foreground refresh, and mutation callbacks are scoped to the signed-in user id.
documented_requirement: A non-creator is either not offered the edit action or told plainly that only the creator can change space details.
A failed save explains the rule and preserves the current values.
The UI never implies that the partner's change was saved.
hypothetical_user_behavior:
A fictional participant (Nadia Iqbal) said: "Walked through device recovery as I actually use it — one-handed, on a train, thumb only. Answers to "why does this even exist?"

1. The recovery-phrase *check* (the "re-type words 3, 7, 11" step). It exists to prove I wrote it down. But it proves I can copy 3 words off a screen I'm still looking at. It doesn't catch the real failure (phrase written down wrong, or photographed into a camera roll). Remove it: nothing breaks. The phrase itself is the artifact; the quiz is theater. Cost: two extra screens, one of which I've fat-fingered and had to restart.

2. Trust codes. I have never once compared them out loud with anyone. In a two-person space there's no untrusted third party to verify against, so the code is a ritual that answers a question nobody asked. Remove: the pairing flow loses a step and loses nothing else. If verification ever matters, do it silently and tell me only on mismatch.

3. The device list. Not because device management is useless — because *this* one is a list I can't act on. It shows me a device, a name, a last-seen, and then... nothing that resolves anything. It's a status page pretending to be a control. If a device is compromised, what do I do, stare at it? Remove the list as-is; keep it only if revoking is one tap from the row.

The one I'd keep: the warning on the restore path that says plainly what gets destroyed and what survives. It's the only place in the whole flow that told me the truth before I committed instead of after.

Bonus, since you said every helper line: the spinner on save. A spinner is not a state. Pending, succeeded, and failed need to look different — right now they all look like patience. And the disabled Continue button with no reason attached is the same bug wearing a gray shirt."
Nadia Iqbal assumes: a disabled button explains why
Nadia Iqbal assumes: a save has a visible pending and failure state
Theo Bennett assumes: a pending upload is visibly pending
Theo Bennett assumes: a six-character code accepts a pasted message
